items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: Ray Lopez, comma, Larry Shields, comma, Illinois, Canada, and William Lambert were in the band with me.

ctx.x: Their champion was a colored man. Let's say a colored man has his rightful place in any music. Why not the white man to eulogize another man that hasn't created anything because of his color? That must be his music. But although Elvin Presley went on to hikes while the other guy stayed there, if you listen to his style, he couldn't have been original because he changed four or five different times. First his rhythm was based on the tango. Then he changed it to something else. Elvin Presley stuck to one style and…

This is a letter. Headed Paris, December 16, 1956. Dear Mr. LaRocca, The very long trip I have done through the world is at its end. I am just arrived from Melbourne this morning with a great regret not to have been in New Orleans for meeting you. But fate is blind and can offer me a very next opportunity to go to the States for another film. I suppose you have well received my letter dated November the 11th that I have sent you from Calcutta. If you don't, I will mail you a copy. The 1956 Olympic Games were very…

Cafe what wonderful music the Tom Brown Band had, and he wired us an offer to play at his place. The price was right, I'm sorry, to play at his place, period. The price was right and we accepted the job, period. That is how this dance team helped give our music a start, period. They were the first ones to tell Chicago about the Browns Dixieland Band, period. items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: The original band, Brown's band consisted of Gussie Miller, clarinet, lamb and drums, light piano guitar, Steve Brown bass, Tom Brown trombone, and Ray Lopez carnit. That was the original band.

ctx.x: I'll write you again soon. I wish to you and your family a very good Happy New Year. And Holly Expus, your friend J.C. Avoté, and he signs it Jean C. Avoté. P.S. You will find in this letter the results of my investigations in the New York newspapers between 1915 and 1919. What he means about his typewriter is that he wrote the E key and he has to put acute marks and grave marks on his E's. It's the only way he can finish a letter.

Well, he wrote down to Mr. Howard Jacobs. He put a piece in the paper for asking for an old time jazz band to write him. That he was trying to clear up the great mystery that hangs over the jazz. That someone should get credit where it should be. Now many people ask, amongst this one was this Tom Brown and the record changer. Well, now these things I had never known before, the record changer, the claims that Brown made. These had just come to my mind. Now when you have a family to support you, just don't jump up…

It says, uh, CCE, DJ LaRocca, number 2218 Constant Street. October the 14th, 1957, I see. Heading of the letter, Mr. Harry V. Sushant, comma, President, New Orleans Jazz Club, comma, 2417 Octavia Street, New Orleans, Louisiana. Dear Harry, colon, for many months now, comma, I have delayed writing you concerning a matter, a matter, that I know means a great deal to you and the members of your organization, period.
